# ETF Selection Notes

## Overview

My broker's dealing screen lists just over 2,400 products when I open it with no filter at all, a number that includes every share class, every currency line and a long tail of funds nobody should buy. The first minute is spent cutting that list down rather than reading it. I filter to funds, drop the ones without a five-year history, and sort by the index family I already understand. What is left is usually sixty or seventy rows, and the real comparison starts there. I do this once a quarter rather than weekly, because nothing on that screen changes fast enough to deserve a daily look, and the whole exercise is about patience rather than timing. The screen also remembers a watchlist, which is where the shortlisted rows go so I can compare them side by side instead of holding numbers in my head.

Next I look at the spread I would pay on the exchange, because that is a real cost every time I deal and it never appears in the headline charge. A developed-market equity fund with a deep book often quotes a spread of a few basis points, while a narrow thematic product can show ten times that. I check the spread at the open and again an hour later, since the first prints of the day are the widest and the least representative of the rest. For an order I intend to place once and hold for years, a wide spread is a small tax, but I still want to know what it is before I move.

Tracking difference is the figure I trust most, because it is what the wrapper actually cost me. I look at it over three years and over five years rather than one, since a single year can flatter a fund for reasons that will not repeat. A good tracker keeps the gap to twenty or thirty basis points, and a large one tells me that the machinery is leaking: withholding tax, expensive sampling or a clumsy replication method. I read the provider's own reports when the published number is missing.

Share class comes next. Accumulating classes reinvest dividends inside the fund, which spares me the job of putting small payouts back to work, and distributing classes pay them out, which suits an account where I want the income now. Inside a tax wrapper I lean to accumulating; outside one, the choice leans on how the local tax office treats each. I check the class code twice, because two rows next to each other on the screen can differ only by that single letter.

Domicile affects the tax taken from dividends before they ever reach me. The gap between an Irish-domiciled fund and a US-domiciled one can quietly cost or save a chunk each year, and it has nothing to do with how the fund invests. I pick the domicile deliberately and I keep a note of why, because the answer changes with the tax treaty and not with my mood.

Fund size matters for survival. A very small fund carries closure risk, and if assets drop below a workable level the provider may merge or shut it, which forces a sale and a fresh start elsewhere. I look for a fund that has run for at least five years with steady assets, and I check whether the provider has a habit of closing niche products.

I also ask how long the fund has tracked its index without changing it. A provider that quietly swaps the benchmark, or reroutes a fund onto a cheaper index to cut costs, resets the history and can leave me holding a product I never chose. A mandate that has been unchanged for a decade is worth more to me than a slightly lower headline charge.

The order book tells me how easily I can deal. I look at the depth on both sides and the number of market makers, because a thin book means my own order shifts the price against me. For a fund I intend to hold for years this matters little at the margin, but on a small exchange-traded product it can add more than the annual charge in a single trade.

For a plain developed-market equity product I expect a total expense ratio around 0.07%, and I treat anything well above that as a question rather than a verdict: sometimes the extra buys something real, often it does not. Read against the tracking difference, that one number tells me most of what matters before I commit. Bonds are a separate decision that I keep to one side, because duration and credit deserve their own reading rather than a row on this screen.

## Notes

Before buying anything I open the factsheet, not the marketing page, and I check the index it claims to track against the name on the row. I also compare the platform charge, because a cheap fund sitting on an expensive platform is not cheap at all. For a small trade the spread is the cost that bites: on a 500 EUR order a five-basis-point spread is a couple of euros, while a thirty-basis-point spread on the same order is real money. I keep a watchlist in the broker app and I check the spread at a calm hour rather than in the first minutes of the session. Finally I read the ongoing charge and the tracking difference together, and I write the pair of numbers in a note so I can see in a year whether the fund has held its side of the bargain. I also check that the fund still trades at the size I need: a book that was deep when I bought can thin out after the provider changes an index or loses assets, and a thin book costs me more on the way out than it did on the way in. When the numbers hold, I leave the position alone for another quarter rather than finding a reason to trade.

## Troubleshooting

Three problems turn up again and again. The first is a fund that changed its index: the name stays the same, the mandate shifts, and the history no longer describes what I hold. I catch it by comparing the current factsheet with the note I wrote when I bought, and if the mandate has changed I decide afresh rather than drift along with it. The second is a wide spread at the open, which is normal for the first prints of the day; I wait an hour and check again before I deal. The third is a mislabelled share class, where the row on the screen says accumulating and the factsheet says distributing. I read the class code on both and stay out until the two agree. A fourth, rarer case is a fund that stops reporting a tracking difference at all, which usually means a change in the provider or the reporting wrapper; I ask the platform rather than assume the figure is fine.
